doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Jazz parties and the level of playing
summary: Jazz parties offer top-level musicians, unlike local gigs with unfamiliar players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Let me ask you about these jazz parties for a moment. It’s a pretty desirable thing to have in your plate of gigs?

Oh, yeah, by all means. Strictly for the chance to meet people who comprise the jazz audience, that’s one thing, but the main thing is the quality of the musicians. You come to a thing like this, and you know that everyone that you’re going to be playing with is at a certain level, because you think about the axiom that a band is only as good as its worst player, which I believe to be true, given that being an accurate axiom, the lowest level of musicianship here is very high so you are never in a situation where you just can’t get off the ground. The kind of things that happen on your own local scene wherever you are and you’re working with people you never even met or a lot of times don’t even have the same kinds of records in your collection. I mean I did a gig with a Brazilian singer not too long ago, and we couldn’t communicate — even tune titles were very hard to get straight between his Portuguese and my English. And we settled on a whole bunch of Jobim songs, and that was fine, but he knew a whole bunch of other stuff that I just had to play by ear. I just had to go by — that’s a one chord, a six chord, a four chord and then the three chord. You have to default to just like technical ideas rather than — I don’t know their culture that good. I’m not steeped in that culture. I’m not trying to be an exponent of that. So now when he’s back on my turf I take charge, we play some blues or a bebop tune or something, and he would play second fiddle.
